question: What proportion of ambulance-to-emergency-department patient handovers are completed within 15 minutes of the ambulance arriving?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance handover timing has been published in the library, despite this being the single most reported pre-hospital patient-safety problem in England.

standard.source: AACE, Hospital Handovers (webpage, accessed 2026)
standard.wording: The nationally defined target for hospitals included in the NHS Standard Contract states that all handovers between ambulance and A&E must take place within 15 minutes, with none waiting more than 30 minutes.

population: Inclusion: all adult and paediatric patients brought to the ED by a NHS ambulance over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients brought by non-emergency patient transport service, self-presenting or brought by police/other agency
sample: 50 consecutive ambulance arrivals over 2 weeks, using the ambulance service's own arrival timestamp and the ED's handover-accepted timestamp
data_source: Ambulance electronic patient record (arrival time) matched to the ED tracking system (handover-accepted or 'patient in department' time)

template.note: number of patients in the department at the time of arrival, if available

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a rapid 'streaming and handover' nurse and a cohorting bay so incoming ambulances are met at the door, with a visible countdown clock at the ambulance entrance and an internal professional standard escalation when handover passes 30 minutes.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months using the same 2-week sampling window and template
close_loop: Present at the joint ED-ambulance trust liaison meeting; if the streaming nurse role works, make it a permanent rostered post and add handover time to the trust's monthly urgent and emergency care dashboard
evidence: No closed-loop audit of ambulance-to-ED handover timing is in the library; nearest related entries concern ED waiting times and flow
pitfalls: Ambulance and ED clocks are not synchronised → agree a single timestamp source before cycle 1
Small numbers on quiet shifts hide the true delay → sample across day, evening and night shifts
Definition of 'handover accepted' drifts between cycles → lock the definition (first ED clinician contact) in writing with the ambulance trust liaison
Ambulance and nursing staff see this as blame-shifting → present it jointly as a shared flow problem, not a performance league table
Gains fade once the streaming nurse post is not backfilled on leave → build it into the establishment, not a rota extra
pearls: Recruit the ambulance trust liaison officer as a co-presenter before cycle 1
Agree the timestamp definitions with both organisations in writing before data collection starts
Display live handover times on the department screen so staff see the effect of the change in real time
Link the audit to the trust's existing corridor-care or ambulance-queue safety huddle so it does not need a new meeting
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the ambulance and ED electronic records
pass: Ambulance clock-stop (patient accepted by an ED clinician) is within 15 minutes of the ambulance's arrival time recorded on the ambulance electronic patient record

question: What proportion of ambulance pre-alert calls for adult major trauma patients record all the core information items required by the trauma network?
why: No closed-loop audit of pre-alert content quality has been published in the library; incomplete pre-alerts delay trauma team assembly and equipment preparation.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: service delivery, rec 1.8.1 (2016)
standard.wording: Record the following in patients with major trauma in pre-hospital settings: ... the ambulance call sign, name of the person taking the call and time of call.

population: Inclusion: all adult patients brought in as a pre-alerted trauma call over a 4-week period. Exclusion: patients arriving unannounced with trauma subsequently identified
sample: 40 consecutive pre-alerted adult trauma calls over 4 weeks
data_source: Trauma call proforma/EPR trauma page compared against the recorded ambulance radio pre-alert message (call recording or written pre-alert sheet)
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Replace the free-text pre-alert radio message with a structured ATMIST (age, time, mechanism, injuries, signs, treatment) proforma shared with the ambulance trust, printed automatically as a trauma call sheet when the pre-alert is logged.
target: ≥90% of pre-alerts complete on all items
reaudit: Re-audit at 4 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the joint trauma network governance meeting with the ambulance trust; embed the ATMIST proforma in both the ambulance despatch system and the ED trauma call sheet if it improves completeness
evidence: ONA-024 and ONA-026 (pelvic fracture care) show ambulance-to-hospital information sharing already matters in this network; no audit of pre-alert content completeness itself is in the library
pitfalls: Radio recordings are hard to retrieve after a few days → agree a retrieval process with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Small sample if trauma calls are infrequent → extend the collection window to 6 weeks in a lower-volume unit
Definitions of 'given' vary between reviewers → agree a one-page scoring key before starting
Ambulance crews may feel audited without being consulted → involve the trust's trauma desk lead in designing the proforma
Improvement fades once new crews rotate in → add ATMIST training to ambulance trust induction
pearls: Get sign-off from the trauma network's clinical lead before starting, since the change affects the ambulance trust too
Use existing trauma network governance meetings to close the loop rather than creating a new forum
Pilot the ATMIST proforma on one ambulance station before a wider rollout
Keep the same reviewer for both cycles to reduce scoring drift
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from the trauma proforma and call recordings
pass: The recorded pre-alert (written or on the trauma call proforma) contains mechanism of injury, injuries found, vital signs, treatment given, estimated time of arrival, and the ambulance call sign/name of caller/time of call

question: What proportion of pre-alerted major trauma patients have a trauma team leader and team ready to receive the handover before the patient arrives?
why: No closed-loop audit of trauma team readiness at handover has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: service delivery, recs 1.8.4 and 1.8.5 (2016)
standard.wording: A senior nurse or trauma team leader in the emergency department should receive the pre-alert information and determine the level of trauma team response according to agreed and written local guidelines. The trauma team leader should be easily identifiable to receive the handover and the trauma team ready to receive the information.

population: Inclusion: all pre-alerted adult and paediatric trauma calls over 4 weeks. Exclusion: unannounced trauma arrivals
sample: 40 consecutive pre-alerted trauma calls over 4 weeks
data_source: Trauma call log/EPR trauma page and direct observation or debrief sheet completed by the trauma team leader
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a mandatory trauma team leader tabard and a pre-arrival checklist (bay, airway trolley, blood products requested, team roles assigned) signed off by the TTL before the patient arrives, triggered automatically by the pre-alert bleep.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the trauma governance meeting; if the checklist works, add it as a mandatory step in the trauma call bleep system
evidence: No audit of trauma team readiness at handover is in the library; ONA-024/ONA-026 show related pelvic-trauma pathway gaps
pitfalls: Readiness is hard to verify retrospectively → use direct observation for at least half the sample
Staff may complete the checklist after the event to look compliant → timestamp the checklist electronically
Small numbers if major trauma calls are rare → extend the collection window
Rota gaps mean no consultant TTL is available out of hours → escalate staffing gaps found by the audit to rota planning
Improvement fades once the tabard goes missing → keep a spare stock in the resus room
pearls: Recruit the trauma coordinator to help design and pilot the checklist
Agree with nursing and ED consultant leads before cycle 1 who owns team readiness
Use the trauma governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the audit tool the same across cycles so the readiness rate is directly comparable
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the trauma log and direct observation
pass: A named trauma team leader is recorded as having received the pre-alert, and the trauma bay/team is documented as ready (equipment checked, team present) before the patient's arrival

question: What proportion of adults with major trauma needing pre-hospital rapid sequence induction have it started within 45 minutes of the initial 999 call?
why: No closed-loop audit of pre-hospital RSI timing has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.2.3 (2016)
standard.wording: Aim to perform RSI as soon as possible and within 45 minutes of the initial call to the emergency services, preferably at the scene of the incident.

population: Inclusion: adults with major trauma who cannot maintain their own airway and/or ventilation and who receive pre-hospital RSI by a critical care team. Exclusion: RSI performed in hospital only
sample: 20 consecutive pre-hospital RSIs over 3 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance/critical care paramedic or HEMS patient report form, cross-checked against the 999 call log time
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Feed back individual case timelines to the regional critical care/HEMS desk at the monthly trauma governance meeting, with a standard 'time to RSI' field added to the electronic patient report form so delays are flagged automatically.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition and template
close_loop: Present at the regional trauma network's pre-hospital governance meeting; if the ePR field works, ask the ambulance trust to make it a standard audit field
evidence: No audit of pre-hospital RSI timing is in the library; ONA-026 (pelvic fracture TXA timing) shows the same network already audits pre-hospital time-critical interventions
pitfalls: 999 call time and drug administration time are recorded on different systems → agree the linkage method with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Small numbers because pre-hospital RSI is rare → pool data across a longer period or across the regional network
Case-mix varies (rural versus urban scenes) → record scene location type to interpret outliers
Crews may feel individually blamed for system delays → present aggregated, anonymised timelines only
Improvement is not sustained after staff turnover on the critical care desk → build the RSI-time review into the desk's standard handover
pearls: Agree data-sharing with the ambulance/critical care service before starting, since most of the data sits outside the hospital
Recruit the regional trauma network's pre-hospital lead as co-owner of the audit
Use the existing trauma governance meeting to close the loop
Keep case numbers pooled across the network if a single trust's volume is too small to interpret alone
effort: ~30 min per case from the ambulance/HEMS patient report form
pass: Time from the initial 999 call to RSI drug administration (scene or en route) is 45 minutes or less

question: What proportion of adults with active pre-hospital haemorrhage who receive intravenous fluid are given crystalloid only when blood components are not available?
why: No closed-loop audit of pre-hospital fluid choice in active bleeding has been published in the library; inappropriate crystalloid use can worsen coagulopathy.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.5.22 (2016)
standard.wording: In pre-hospital settings only use crystalloids to replace fluid volume in patients with active bleeding if blood components are not available.

population: Inclusion: adults with active bleeding from trauma who receive any IV fluid pre-hospital. Exclusion: patients with no fluid given, or fluid given only after blood products started
sample: 30 consecutive pre-hospital trauma patients with active bleeding who received IV fluid, over 3 months
data_source: Ambulance/HEMS patient report form fluid administration record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'blood available: yes/no, reason for crystalloid' field to the ambulance/HEMS electronic patient report form fluid section, and reinforce the crystalloid-avoidance message in the trauma network's annual pre-hospital update training.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the regional trauma network pre-hospital governance meeting; embed the mandatory field in the ambulance ePR if it improves practice
evidence: No audit of pre-hospital fluid choice in active bleeding is in the library; ONA-026 (pelvic fracture TXA) is the nearest related pre-hospital trauma audit
pitfalls: Free-text fluid records make coding inconsistent → agree a coding key with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Blood component availability varies by crew type, confounding comparisons → record crew type for every case
Small numbers if pre-hospital blood is well established locally → pool across the network
Crews may see this as second-guessing a scene decision → frame feedback as system learning, not individual performance
Gains fade if new crews are not told about the change → add to annual mandatory pre-hospital training
pearls: Involve the ambulance trust's clinical governance lead from the start
Use the trauma network's existing pre-hospital blood programme meeting to close the loop
Keep the same fluid-choice coding key for both cycles
Share results with crews as a learning bulletin, not a performance table
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the ambulance/HEMS patient report form
pass: Crystalloid is given to a bleeding trauma patient only when the ambulance/HEMS crew records that blood components were not carried or not available at the time

question: What proportion of adults with a head injury and a GCS of 12 or less, and no suspected extracranial bleeding, receive tranexamic acid within 2 hours of injury?
why: No closed-loop audit of tranexamic acid timing in isolated head injury has been published in the library; the nearest related entries concern TXA in pelvic fracture.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.17 (2023)
standard.wording: For people with a head injury and a GCS score of 12 or less who are not thought to have active extracranial bleeding, consider: a 2 g intravenous bolus injection of tranexamic acid for people 16 and over ... Give the tranexamic acid as soon as possible within 2 hours of the injury, in the pre-hospital or hospital setting and before imaging.

population: Inclusion: adults with GCS 12 or less after head injury and no suspected extracranial bleeding, seen pre-hospital or in ED within 2 hours of injury. Exclusion: known contraindication documented at triage (e.g. injury time unknown, >2 hours ago)
sample: 30 consecutive eligible adults over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form and ED trauma clerking, cross-checked against the recorded time of injury and time of TXA administration
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add TXA as a default prompt on both the ambulance head injury pathway card and the ED trauma order set whenever GCS 12 or less is entered without a bleeding flag, with the 2-hour deadline shown on the prompt.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition and template
close_loop: Present at the trauma governance meeting; if the prompt works, add it to both the ambulance clinical decision support tool and the ED EPR trauma order set permanently
evidence: ONA-026 (pelvic fracture TXA within 1 hour) shows a closed-loop audit of TXA timing already works in this network for a different injury; no equivalent audit exists for isolated head injury
pitfalls: Time of injury is often uncertain → exclude or flag cases with an estimated rather than witnessed injury time
Ambulance and ED records are on separate systems → agree a single audit form covering both before cycle 1
Small numbers in a district general hospital → extend the collection period to 6-12 months
Clinicians may worry about giving TXA before imaging excludes a contraindication → reinforce the NICE wording ('before imaging') in training
Gains fade if the prompt is switched off during a system upgrade → check it after any EPR update
pearls: Agree with the ambulance trust which record system will supply the injury-time and TXA-time fields before starting
Recruit a trauma nurse coordinator to flag eligible cases prospectively as a data-collection aid
Present pooled ambulance and hospital data together so both services see the whole pathway
Keep the same eligibility criteria (GCS ≤12, no extracranial bleeding) across cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and ED records
pass: TXA 2 g IV bolus is given, or a documented reason for not giving it is recorded, within 2 hours of injury

question: What proportion of ambulance patient report forms for head-injured children and adults record a Glasgow Coma Scale score using the correct adult or paediatric version?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance GCS recording accuracy has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.15 (2003)
standard.wording: Ambulance crews and paramedics should be fully trained in the use of the adult and paediatric versions of the GCS and its derived score.

population: Inclusion: all patients conveyed by ambulance after a head injury over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients with no ambulance patient report form available
sample: 40 consecutive ambulance-conveyed head injury patients over 2 weeks
data_source: Ambulance patient report form handed over with the patient, or the ambulance trust's electronic record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Feed back examples of incomplete or wrong-version GCS recording to the ambulance trust's clinical education team for inclusion in the next mandatory update training cycle, and add a hard-stop prompt for the paediatric GCS version in the electronic patient report form for patients under 5.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present jointly to the ED and ambulance trust clinical governance leads; if the electronic prompt reduces errors, keep it as a permanent build
evidence: No audit of ambulance GCS recording accuracy is in the library; ONA-163 shows the same trauma network already audits documentation quality for head injury in children
pitfalls: Ambulance and hospital notes may be scored differently by different reviewers → use one trained reviewer for the whole audit
Paediatric cases are infrequent, giving small numbers → extend the sampling period for the under-5 subgroup
Ambulance crews may feel individually singled out → report results in aggregate only
Definitions of 'correct version' can be disputed at the 5-year-old boundary → agree the cut-off with the ambulance trust in advance
Improvement is not sustained after a change of electronic patient record supplier → re-check the prompt after any system change
pearls: Agree access to ambulance patient report forms with the ambulance trust's information governance team before starting
Involve the ambulance trust's clinical education lead in interpreting results
Use existing joint governance meetings rather than creating a new one
Keep the same scoring key across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ambulance patient report form
pass: A GCS score (eye, verbal, motor and total) is recorded on the ambulance patient report form, using the paediatric GCS for children under 5 and the standard GCS for everyone else

question: When ambulance crews identify a safeguarding concern in a patient with a head injury, what proportion of cases have this documented and verbally handed over to the emergency department?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance-to-ED safeguarding handover has been published in the library, despite this being an explicit training requirement.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.16 (2003, amended 2014)
standard.wording: Ambulance crews and paramedics should be trained in the safeguarding of people under 16 and people 16 and over who are vulnerable. They should document and verbally inform emergency department staff of any safeguarding concerns.

population: Inclusion: all patients arriving with a head injury by ambulance whose patient report form flags a safeguarding concern (non-accidental injury suspicion, vulnerable adult, self-neglect, frequent falls in a vulnerable adult) over 3 months. Exclusion: no safeguarding flag on the ambulance form
sample: 20 consecutive flagged cases over 3 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form safeguarding section, matched to the ED clerking/triage note and the trust safeguarding referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'ambulance safeguarding flag received: yes/no, action taken' field to the ED triage template, so a flagged case cannot be booked in without an ED safeguarding decision being recorded.
target: 100% of flagged cases have a documented ED safeguarding decision
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the trust safeguarding committee jointly with the ambulance trust designated safeguarding lead; if the mandatory field works, keep it permanently in the triage template
evidence: No audit of ambulance-to-ED safeguarding handover for head injury is in the library; NNA-089 (adolescent mental health assessment) shows the same department already audits vulnerable-patient pathway gaps
pitfalls: Safeguarding flags on ambulance forms are often free text and easy to miss at triage → make the field mandatory rather than free text
Small numbers given expected low case volume → extend the collection period to 6 months
Information governance restrictions on accessing ambulance safeguarding data → agree data-sharing with the ambulance trust's safeguarding lead first
Staff may under-report to avoid extra paperwork → make the field quick (drop-down, not free text)
Loop closure stalls if the safeguarding committee meets infrequently → agree a fixed re-audit slot on the agenda in advance
pearls: Involve both trusts' safeguarding leads from the outset, since this is a cross-organisational pathway
Use the existing safeguarding committee to close the loop rather than a new meeting
Keep the case definition (types of flag counted) identical across cycles
Share anonymised case learning, not identifiable feedback, with individual crews
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and ED records
pass: Where the ambulance patient report form records a safeguarding concern, the ED clerking or triage note documents that the concern was verbally handed over and an ED safeguarding action was taken (referral, discussion with named nurse, or documented reason not to act)

question: What proportion of adults with suspected acute stroke conveyed by ambulance are admitted directly to a specialist acute stroke unit without first going to a general emergency department bay?
why: No closed-loop audit of direct ambulance-to-stroke-unit conveyance has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG128 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, rec 1.3.1 (2008)
standard.wording: Admit everyone with suspected stroke directly to a specialist acute stroke unit after initial assessment, from either the community, the emergency department, or outpatient clinics.

population: Inclusion: adults brought by ambulance with a positive pre-hospital stroke screen (e.g. FAST-positive) over a 4-week period. Exclusion: stroke diagnosed after arrival with no pre-hospital stroke screen documented
sample: 30 consecutive FAST-positive ambulance conveyances over 4 weeks
data_source: Ambulance patient report form (FAST screen result and pre-alert), ED tracking system (bed location) and stroke unit admission log

options: General ED bay then stroke unit
General ED bay only, not admitted to stroke unit

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree a direct-conveyance protocol with the ambulance trust so a FAST-positive pre-alert triggers the stroke unit bed to be held and the patient taken straight there (bypassing the general ED cubicle) unless immediate resuscitation is needed.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition and template
close_loop: Present at the stroke network's operational delivery network meeting with ambulance trust representation; embed the direct-conveyance protocol in the ambulance dispatch system if it improves the rate
evidence: NNA-119/NNA-120 (TIA aspirin and CT decision-making) show this network already audits stroke and TIA pathway steps in the ED; no audit of ambulance-to-stroke-unit direct conveyance is in the library
pitfalls: Bed availability on the stroke unit may block direct conveyance regardless of the pathway → record bed availability as a separate field
Small numbers in a unit without a hyperacute stroke service → adjust the pathway definition to the local model of care
FAST-positive pre-alerts may be over- or under-called → cross check against the final stroke/TIA/stroke-mimic diagnosis
ED staff may resist bypassing initial ED assessment → involve ED consultants in agreeing exceptions (e.g. unstable airway) in advance
Gains fade if the stroke unit's bed-holding process is not maintained → review bed-holding capacity at the re-audit
pearls: Agree the direct-conveyance protocol jointly with ambulance, ED and stroke medicine before cycle 1
Use the stroke operational delivery network meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Track bed availability as a confounder so failures to bypass are not all attributed to the pathway
Keep the FAST-positive definition identical across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and stroke unit records
pass: The patient's first inpatient bed after ambulance arrival is the acute/hyperacute stroke unit, or a documented reason is recorded for going elsewhere (for example, needing immediate resuscitation)

question: What proportion of adults with an ambulance-diagnosed ST-elevation myocardial infarction receive a 300 mg aspirin loading dose before hospital arrival?
why: No closed-loop audit of pre-hospital aspirin administration in STEMI has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes, rec 1.1.4 (2010)
standard.wording: Offer people with acute STEMI a single loading dose of 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible unless there is clear evidence that they are allergic to it.

population: Inclusion: adults with a pre-hospital 12-lead ECG diagnosis of STEMI conveyed by ambulance over 3 months. Exclusion: cardiac arrest before aspirin could be given
sample: 30 consecutive ambulance-diagnosed STEMI patients over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form medication record, cross-checked with the cardiac catheter laboratory admission proforma
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Feed back cases where aspirin was omitted or delayed to the ambulance trust's cardiac clinical lead, and add a mandatory 'aspirin given: dose/time or reason not given' field to the ambulance STEMI pathway record.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the cardiac network's primary PCI governance meeting with ambulance trust representation; embed the mandatory field permanently if compliance improves
evidence: NNA-384 (angiography timing in NSTEMI) shows this network already audits ACS pathway timings in hospital; no audit of pre-hospital aspirin administration in STEMI is in the library
pitfalls: Patients who self-medicate with aspirin before the ambulance arrives may be miscounted → record 'already taken' as a separate category
Small numbers of pre-hospital STEMI diagnoses in a smaller ambulance sector → pool data across the cardiac network
Allergy documentation is sometimes missing rather than a true contraindication → distinguish 'documented allergy' from 'not recorded'
Crews may feel blamed for a system-level cath lab bottleneck → keep the audit focused on the aspirin step only
Gains fade if the mandatory field is removed in a system update → recheck after any ambulance ePR change
pearls: Agree data access with the ambulance trust's cardiac clinical lead before starting
Use the cardiac network's existing primary PCI governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the STEMI diagnosis definition (ambulance 12-lead ECG criteria) identical across cycles
Share results as a learning bulletin for crews, not a named performance table
effort: ~15 min per case from the ambulance patient report form
pass: 300 mg aspirin is given by the ambulance crew (or already taken and confirmed) before hospital arrival, or a documented allergy/contraindication is recorded

question: What proportion of adults who achieve return of spontaneous circulation after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest have their oxygen saturation titrated to 94-98% by the time of ED handover?
why: No closed-loop audit of post-ROSC oxygen titration during ambulance transfer has been published in the library, despite hyperoxaemia and hypoxaemia both being harmful after cardiac arrest.

standard.source: Resuscitation Council UK, Post-resuscitation care guidelines (2021, updated July 2023)
standard.wording: After ROSC, once SpO2 can be measured reliably or arterial blood gas values are obtained, titrate the inspired oxygen to achieve an arterial oxygen saturation of 94-98% ... Avoid hypoxaemia ... Avoid hyperoxaemia following ROSC.

population: Inclusion: adults with sustained ROSC after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest conveyed by ambulance over 6 months. Exclusion: death before ED arrival, re-arrest during transfer with no further ROSC
sample: 20 consecutive ROSC patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form observations chart, cross-checked with the ED resuscitation room record at handover
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'post-ROSC oxygen target 94-98%' prompt to the ambulance cardiac arrest care bundle card and the post-ROSC section of the electronic patient report form, so oxygen is actively titrated down once saturations are reliably measured.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the cardiac arrest network's post-resuscitation care governance meeting with the ambulance trust; embed the prompt permanently in the ambulance care bundle card if it improves the target rate
evidence: No audit of post-ROSC oxygen titration during ambulance transfer is in the library; the nearest related entries concern oxygen prescribing with target saturations in the ED
pitfalls: Pulse oximetry can be unreliable in a cold, shut-down post-arrest patient → record whether the SpO2 reading was judged reliable
Small numbers given expected low ROSC volume → extend the collection period or pool with a neighbouring ambulance sector
Crews may keep FiO2 high out of caution → reinforce the harm of hyperoxaemia in training, not just hypoxaemia
Definitions of 'reliable SpO2' vary → agree a working definition with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Gains fade without refresher training after the initial rollout → add to the annual post-resuscitation care update
pearls: Link the audit to the trust's existing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes review meeting
Recruit a resuscitation officer from both the ambulance trust and the ED as joint audit leads
Keep the SpO2 target and 'reliable reading' definitions identical for both cycles
Feed results back through the ambulance trust's cardiac arrest governance process, which already exists
effort: ~15 min per case from ambulance and ED resuscitation records
pass: The last recorded SpO2 before ED handover is 94-98%, or a documented reason for a different target is recorded (for example, known chronic respiratory disease with a lower target)

question: What proportion of adults with return of spontaneous circulation after cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause are transported directly to a hospital with 24/7 primary PCI capability?
why: No closed-loop audit of direct conveyance to a cardiac arrest/heart attack centre after ROSC has been published in the library.

standard.source: Resuscitation Council UK, Post-resuscitation care guidelines (2021, updated July 2023)
standard.wording: Adult patients with a cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac aetiology should be transported directly to a hospital with 24/7 coronary angiography capability.

population: Inclusion: adults with sustained ROSC after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest thought to be of cardiac cause, over 6 months. Exclusion: cardiac arrest with an obvious non-cardiac cause (trauma, drowning, hanging)
sample: 20 consecutive eligible ROSC patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance patient report form destination decision record and receiving hospital's cardiac arrest centre admission log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Agree a documented destination-decision algorithm with the ambulance trust's cardiac arrest desk so presumed-cardiac ROSC cases bypass the nearest general ED and go directly to the network's 24/7 PCI centre unless airway or scene factors prevent it.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition and template
close_loop: Present at the out-of-hospital cardiac arrest network governance meeting with ambulance trust representation; if the destination algorithm reduces onward transfers, adopt it as standard ambulance dispatch policy
evidence: No audit of direct post-ROSC conveyance to a PCI centre is in the library; NNA-384 (angiography timing in NSTEMI) shows the same network already audits related cardiac pathway timings
pitfalls: Presumed cardiac cause is a judgement call and can be coded inconsistently → agree the coding criteria with ambulance clinicians before cycle 1
Rural areas may have long transfer times to the PCI centre → record transfer distance as a confounder
Small numbers given expected low ROSC volume → pool data across the network if a single ambulance sector is too small
Onward inter-hospital transfers add delay and risk if the algorithm is not followed → track onward transfers as a secondary outcome
Improvement is not sustained if the algorithm is not built into ambulance dispatch software → make it a system default rather than a memory-based decision

question: What proportion of adults with suspected sepsis who are discharged from the ED after a period of observation have a documented safety-netting plan given to them in writing?

change: Add a mandatory 'sepsis safety-netting leaflet given' tick box to the ED discharge template, linked to an automatic print of the leaflet whenever a sepsis screening tool has been used during the attendance.

question: What proportion of adults presenting to the ED with an acute exacerbation of COPD have their oxygen prescribed with a target saturation range appropriate to their risk of hypercapnia?

standard.wording: Use a target oxygen saturation range of 88-92% for patients with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who are at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, until blood gas results are available.

data_source: ED drug chart/EPR oxygen prescription and arterial/venous blood gas record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the oxygen target saturation range a mandatory field on the ED electronic drug chart whenever a COPD diagnosis flag is present, defaulting to 88-92% with an override reason required to change it.

question: What proportion of adults with a suspected ectopic pregnancy have a formal transvaginal ultrasound or gynaecology review arranged within 24 hours of presenting to the ED?

standard.source: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management, rec 1.2.4 (2019, updated 2021)
standard.wording: Refer women and pregnant people to an early pregnancy assessment service if they are more than 6 weeks pregnant, or if the gestation is uncertain and they have pain and/or bleeding, or other complications ... to confirm the location and viability of the pregnancy.

change: Add a direct electronic referral route from the ED clerking template to the early pregnancy assessment unit, with a weekend/out-of-hours pathway to on-call gynaecology so referrals made overnight are still seen within 24 hours.

close_loop: Present at the joint ED-gynaecology governance meeting; keep the direct electronic referral route permanently if it improves the 24-hour rate

question: What proportion of adults with suspected acute limb ischaemia in the ED are discussed with the vascular surgery on-call team within 30 minutes of the diagnosis being suspected?

standard.wording: Patients with suspected acute limb ischaemia should be discussed with a vascular surgeon immediately, and those with an ischaemic limb should be assessed by a vascular surgeon within 30 minutes of referral.

question: What proportion of adults triaged as category 2 (very urgent) in the ED are seen by a clinician within 10 minutes of triage?
why: No closed-loop audit of time from triage category to first clinician contact for the most urgent non-resuscitation patients has been published in the library.

standard.source: Manchester Triage Group / RCEM Triage position statement, summarised in RCEM Best Practice Guideline: Triage (2017, reviewed)
standard.wording: Patients triaged as 'very urgent' (category 2) should be seen by a clinician within 10 minutes of arrival at triage.

population: Inclusion: all adults triaged as category 2 over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients who deteriorate to resuscitation status before first clinician contact (already captured by resuscitation-room standards)
sample: 40 consecutive category 2 triage episodes over 2 weeks
data_source: ED tracking system triage-complete and first-clinician-seen timestamps
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a category 2 visual flag and 10-minute countdown to the ED tracking board, with a nurse-in-charge escalation if the countdown expires before a clinician has been assigned.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED patient safety and flow meeting; keep the countdown flag permanently if it improves the 10-minute rate
evidence: ED triage accuracy already has 5 audits in the library, but none measures time from category 2 triage to first clinician contact, which is the outcome that matters for patient safety
pitfalls: Tracking system timestamps can be inaccurate if staff log in retrospectively → spot-check a sample against direct observation
Occupancy pressure is the main driver of delay and is outside the audit's control → record occupancy as a confounder, not an excuse to exclude cases
Small numbers on quiet shifts → sample across day, evening and night shifts
Staff may feel individually blamed for system-level overcrowding → present results as a department-level flow measure, not a named performance table
Gains fade once escalation fatigue sets in during sustained high occupancy → review escalation triggers at the re-audit
pearls: Agree the triage-category definitions with the ED triage lead before starting
Use the department's existing flow/safety huddle to close the loop
Keep the 10-minute definition and category 2 criteria identical across both cycles
Track occupancy alongside compliance so the effect of flow pressure is visible, not hidden
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ED tracking system
pass: Time from triage completion to first clinician (doctor, ACP or ENP) contact is 10 minutes or less for a category 2 patient

question: What proportion of adults discharged from the ED with a new diagnosis of atrial fibrillation have anticoagulation risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) formally assessed before discharge?
why: No closed-loop audit of anticoagulation risk assessment at first ED presentation of atrial fibrillation has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.4.1 (2021)
standard.wording: Use the CHA2DS2-VASc score to assess stroke risk in people with any of the following: symptomatic or asymptomatic paroxysmal, persistent or permanent atrial fibrillation ... atrial flutter ... a continuing risk of arrhythmia recurrence after cardioversion back to sinus rhythm.

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit

Use the joint ED-cardiology governance meeting to close the loop

question: When ambulance crews attend a person who has self-harmed but does not need urgent physical care, what proportion have a documented discussion of the person's care/safety plan and this information passed on if not conveyed?
why: No closed-loop audit of ambulance non-conveyance self-harm care has been published in the library; NNA-088/NNA-145/NNA-146 audit the ED end of the self-harm pathway but not the ambulance non-conveyance decision.

standard.source: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.7.9 (2022)
standard.wording: When attending a person who has self-harmed but who does not need urgent physical care, ambulance staff and paramedics should: discuss with the person the best way that the ambulance service can help them; follow the person's care plan and safety plan if available; seek advice from mental health professionals, where necessary; record relevant information ... and pass this information to staff if the person is conveyed, or share it with other relevant people involved in the person's ongoing care if the person is not being conveyed.

population: Inclusion: adults attended by ambulance following self-harm who did not need urgent physical care, over 3 months. Exclusion: patients conveyed to hospital for physical treatment of the self-harm injury itself
sample: 20 consecutive eligible non-conveyance episodes over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance electronic patient record self-harm/mental health section
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a structured self-harm non-conveyance section to the ambulance electronic patient record with mandatory fields for care/safety plan check, mental health advice sought, and information sharing, linked to a direct referral route to the crisis/home treatment team.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present jointly to the ambulance trust mental health lead and the community mental health governance meeting; embed the structured section permanently if it improves documented information-sharing
evidence: NNA-088, NNA-145 and NNA-146 (self-harm risk rating and discharge in the ED) show this pathway is well audited once patients reach hospital; no audit of the ambulance non-conveyance decision itself is in the library
pitfalls: Non-conveyed episodes are not always separately coded from other 'not conveyed' outcomes → agree a coding filter with the ambulance trust before cycle 1
Care and safety plans may exist in mental health records the ambulance crew cannot access in real time → record whether the crew had access to the plan, not just whether one existed
Small numbers given how this presentation is coded → extend the collection period to 6 months
Crews may under-document sensitive conversations → keep the audit tool short and focused on the specific NG225 items
Gains fade if the crisis team referral route is not resourced → confirm capacity with the crisis team before scaling up
pearls: Involve the ambulance trust's mental health lead and the local crisis team from the start
Use an existing joint mental health/ambulance governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the coding filter for 'self-harm, not conveyed' identical across both cycles
Track whether alternative services were actually accessed, not just discussed, as a secondary outcome
effort: ~15 min per case from the ambulance electronic patient record
pass: The ambulance record documents that the person's existing care/safety plan was checked and followed (or that none existed), and that relevant information was shared with the person's ongoing care team if not conveyed

question: What proportion of pre-hospital chest decompressions for suspected tension pneumothorax are performed only in patients with documented haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise?
why: No closed-loop audit of appropriateness of pre-hospital chest decompression has been published in the library; unnecessary decompression itself causes harm.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.3.4 (2016)
standard.wording: Only perform chest decompression in a patient with suspected tension pneumothorax if there is haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise.

population: Inclusion: all patients who received a pre-hospital needle or open chest decompression for suspected tension pneumothorax, over 6 months. Exclusion: decompression performed after hospital arrival
sample: 15 consecutive pre-hospital chest decompressions over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Ambulance/HEMS/critical care paramedic patient report form
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'indication for decompression: haemodynamic instability / severe respiratory compromise' field to the ambulance/HEMS chest trauma pathway, and reinforce the NG39 threshold in the trauma network's annual pre-hospital training update.
reaudit: Re-audit at 12 months, same sample definition (given expected low case volume)
close_loop: Present at the regional trauma network pre-hospital governance meeting; embed the mandatory field permanently if appropriateness improves

Crews may feel individually scrutinised for a rare, high-stakes decision → present findings in aggregate, with a focus on system learning

Use the trauma governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the indication definitions (haemodynamic instability, severe respiratory compromise) identical across both cycles

pass: The pre-hospital record documents haemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock) or severe respiratory compromise immediately before chest decompression was performed

question: What proportion of adults on warfarin with a head injury and CT-confirmed intracranial haemorrhage receive prothrombin complex concentrate within 1 hour of the scan result?
why: No closed-loop audit of anticoagulation reversal timing in traumatic intracranial haemorrhage has been published in the library; NNA-080 audits the CT-decision step but not reversal once bleeding is confirmed.

standard.source: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.5.13 (2023), cross-referring to NICE's guideline on blood transfusion
standard.wording: For advice on reversing vitamin K antagonists for people with traumatic intracranial haemorrhage, see the section on prothrombin complex concentrate in NICE's guideline on blood transfusion.

change: Build a 'warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage' order set in the ED EPR that fires automatically when a CT report containing both 'intracranial haemorrhage' and an anticoagulant flag is filed, pre-selecting weight-based prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K.

close_loop: Present at the ED and haematology joint governance meeting; embed the automatic order set permanently if time to reversal improves

pass: Prothrombin complex concentrate is prescribed and administered within 1 hour of the CT report confirming intracranial haemorrhage in a patient taking a vitamin K antagonist

question: What proportion of adults with an ambulance-diagnosed STEMI, when the primary PCI centre is not the nearest hospital, are taken directly to the primary PCI centre rather than the nearest emergency department?
why: No closed-loop audit of direct-to-cath-lab bypass decisions for ambulance-diagnosed STEMI has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes, rec 1.1.6 (2013)
standard.wording: Offer coronary angiography, with follow-on primary PCI if indicated, as the preferred coronary reperfusion strategy for people with acute STEMI, if: presentation is within 12 hours of onset of symptoms and primary PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time when fibrinolysis could have been given.

population: Inclusion: adults with a pre-hospital 12-lead ECG diagnosis of STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset, where the nearest hospital is not the primary PCI centre, over 6 months. Exclusion: patients presenting more than 12 hours after symptom onset
sample: 20 consecutive eligible patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)

change: Agree a documented bypass-distance threshold with the ambulance trust and cardiac network so any ambulance-diagnosed STEMI within the threshold travel time bypasses the nearest ED automatically, with the cath lab activated directly from the ambulance ECG transmission.

reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the cardiac network primary PCI governance meeting with ambulance trust representation; adopt the bypass threshold as standard ambulance policy if call-to-balloon times improve

Gains fade if cath lab activation from the ambulance ECG is not reliably actioned → audit cath lab response time alongside conveyance decision
pearls: Agree the bypass-distance threshold jointly with the ambulance trust and cardiac network before starting

effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance and cardiac network records

Keep the 'red feature' definition identical to the one used in the ED for continuity across the pathway
effort: ~15 min per case from the ambulance electronic patient record
pass: A child with a documented NICE 'red' fever feature is conveyed by emergency ambulance immediately (not left at home or referred to a delayed pathway), or a documented clinical reason for an alternative pathway is recorded

question: What proportion of people with sudden-onset neurological symptoms assessed by an ambulance crew have a validated FAST (Face Arm Speech Test) screen documented before hypoglycaemia is excluded and a stroke pre-alert decision is made?
why: No closed-loop audit of the completeness of the pre-hospital FAST and hypoglycaemia-exclusion sequence has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG128 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, recs 1.1.1 and 1.1.2 (2008)
standard.wording: Use a validated tool, such as FAST (Face Arm Speech Test), outside hospital to screen people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms for a diagnosis of stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). Exclude hypoglycaemia in people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms as the cause of these symptoms.

population: Inclusion: adults assessed by ambulance for sudden-onset neurological symptoms over a 2-week period. Exclusion: patients with an obvious alternative cause identified at scene (for example, a witnessed seizure with full recovery)
sample: 30 consecutive eligible ambulance assessments over 2 weeks
data_source: Ambulance electronic patient record neurological assessment section
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make both the FAST score and capillary glucose mandatory fields on the ambulance electronic patient report form before the stroke pre-alert option can be selected, so the sequence cannot be skipped.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present jointly to the ambulance trust and stroke operational delivery network; keep the mandatory field sequence permanently if completeness improves
evidence: No audit of pre-hospital FAST and hypoglycaemia-exclusion completeness is in the library; NNA-119/NNA-120 show this network already audits the hospital-side stroke/TIA pathway
pitfalls: Capillary glucose may be checked but not documented in the neurological assessment section → search the whole ambulance record, not just the stroke-specific field
FAST scoring can be inconsistently applied by less experienced crews → provide a laminated FAST reference card on every vehicle
Small numbers if stroke-call coding is inconsistent → cross-check against the stroke pre-alert log as well as the neurological assessment field
Crews under time pressure may prioritise conveyance speed over full documentation → keep the mandatory fields quick (tick-box, not free text)
Gains fade without refresher training → add to the ambulance trust's annual stroke pathway update
pearls: Agree the mandatory field design with the ambulance trust's stroke clinical lead before starting
Use the stroke operational delivery network meeting, which already exists, to close the loop
Keep the FAST tool and glucose threshold definitions identical across both cycles
Track pre-alert accuracy (stroke mimics versus confirmed stroke) as a secondary measure of the pathway's overall quality
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the ambulance electronic patient record
pass: Both a documented FAST score and a documented capillary blood glucose (excluding hypoglycaemia) are recorded on the ambulance patient report form before the stroke pathway decision is made

question: What proportion of adults with major trauma and active or suspected bleeding who are taking an anticoagulant have a documented decision about reversal made with, or by, a haematologist?
why: No closed-loop audit of haematology involvement in anticoagulation reversal decisions for bleeding trauma patients has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.5.11-1.5.12 (2016)
standard.wording: Do not reverse anticoagulation in patients who do not have active or suspected bleeding. For advice on reversing direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), see the MHRA safety advice on DOACs for a list of reversal agents.

population: Inclusion: adults with major trauma known to be taking an anticoagulant (warfarin, DOAC, heparin) who are admitted via the trauma pathway, over 6 months. Exclusion: patients on antiplatelet monotherapy only
sample: 20 consecutive eligible patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
data_source: Trauma clerking record, haematology consultation note, drug chart/EPMA administration record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'anticoagulant reversal decision: haematology contacted, agent/reason' field to the trauma team clerking proforma whenever an anticoagulant is flagged in the drug history.
reaudit: Re-audit at 6 months, same sample definition
close_loop: Present at the trauma governance and haematology joint meeting; keep the mandatory field permanently if compliance improves
evidence: No audit of haematology involvement in trauma anticoagulation reversal decisions is in the library; the anticoagulated head-injury reversal audit in this set covers a related but narrower (intracranial haemorrhage only) population
pitfalls: Anticoagulant use may not be reliably known at first assessment → cross-check with the GP summary care record and pharmacy medicines reconciliation
Small numbers given expected low volume of anticoagulated major trauma → extend the collection period to 12 months
Out-of-hours haematology advice may be by telephone and not always documented → agree a documentation standard for telephone advice before cycle 1

Reversal may be started before haematology is reached in a genuine emergency, which is appropriate → audit for a subsequent haematology discussion, not necessarily a prior one, in the most urgent cases
Gains fade if the mandatory field is not maintained after an EPR update → recheck after any system change
pearls: Agree the reversal pathway and documentation standard with haematology before starting
Recruit the trauma coordinator to flag eligible cases prospectively
Use the joint trauma-haematology governance meeting to close the loop
Keep the definitions of 'active or suspected bleeding' and 'reversal indicated' identical across both cycles
effort: ~20 min per case from trauma and haematology records
pass: For a bleeding trauma patient on an anticoagulant, the trauma record documents a reversal decision (agent given, or reversal not indicated) made with haematology input; anticoagulation is not reversed in a patient without active or suspected bleeding

question: What proportion of adults triaged in the ED with a pain score of 7 or more (severe pain) receive their first analgesia within 20 minutes of triage?
why: No closed-loop audit of time to first analgesia specifically for severe (rather than any) pain has been published in the library; the corpus's 8 general time-to-analgesia audits do not isolate the severe-pain group most likely to come to harm from delay.

standard.source: Local standard, based on the pain-severity thresholds used in RCEM's Pain in Children quality improvement programme (2021/22) extended to adults
standard.wording: Patients in severe pain (pain score 7 or more out of 10) should receive their first dose of analgesia within 20 minutes of a pain score being recorded.

population: Inclusion: adults triaged with a documented pain score of 7 or more, over 2 weeks. Exclusion: patients who decline analgesia or for whom analgesia is contraindicated and this is documented
sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients over 2 weeks
data_source: ED triage record (pain score, time) and drug chart/EPMA administration time
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a nurse-initiated analgesia protocol at triage for any adult scoring 7 or more, covering oral and intranasal options that do not need a doctor's prescription first.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the ED pain management/patient safety meeting; make the nurse-initiated protocol permanent if it improves the 20-minute rate
evidence: The library holds 8 general time-to-analgesia audits in the ED, none of which isolates the severe (≥7/10) pain-score subgroup, where delay causes the most harm and complaints
pitfalls: Pain scores are not always recorded consistently by all triage staff → audit the recording rate itself as a secondary measure
Nurse-initiated analgesia protocols need pharmacy and governance sign-off before use → secure this before cycle 1
Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across different shift types
Some patients decline analgesia or have a contraindication, which should not count as a breach → record these separately, not as failures
Gains fade if the protocol lapses on renewal → set a renewal reminder alongside the re-audit date
pearls: Agree the nurse-initiated analgesia protocol with pharmacy and medical leadership before starting
Recruit a triage nurse champion to help embed the change
Use the ED pain management meeting, which already exists for other analgesia audits, to close the loop
Keep the pain-score threshold (≥7) and time window identical across both cycles
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from triage and EPMA records
pass: A first dose of analgesia (any route) is given within 20 minutes of a pain score of 7 or more being recorded at triage

question: What proportion of patients whose ambulance handover is delayed beyond 60 minutes have a full set of vital sign observations recorded by ambulance or ED staff at least every 30 minutes while still in the ambulance or queue?
why: No closed-loop audit of observation frequency during prolonged ambulance handover delay has been published in the library, despite a national review finding severe potential harm in this group.

standard.source: AACE, Delayed Hospital Handovers: Impact Assessment of Patient Harm (November 2021), summarised on the AACE Hospital Handovers webpage (accessed 2026)
standard.wording: Over eight in ten of those whose 'handover' (from ambulance clinician to hospital clinician) was delayed beyond 60 minutes were assessed as having potentially experienced some level of harm; 53% low harm, 23% moderate harm and 9% (one patient in ten) could have been said to have experienced severe harm.

population: Inclusion: all patients whose ambulance-to-ED handover exceeds 60 minutes over a 4-week period. Exclusion: handovers under 60 minutes
sample: 20 consecutive handovers exceeding 60 minutes over 4 weeks (or all cases if fewer)
data_source: Ambulance observation chart during the wait, cross-checked with the ED tracking system handover time
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a joint ambulance-ED 'queue safety officer' role during any period when more than 2 ambulances are waiting, responsible for cycling through queued patients to check and escalate observations every 30 minutes.
reaudit: Re-audit at 3 months, same sample size and template
close_loop: Present at the joint ambulance-ED patient safety meeting; make the queue safety officer role permanent during escalation if it improves observation compliance
evidence: This set's ambulance-to-ED handover time audit measures the 15-minute target itself; no audit in the library measures clinical monitoring quality during a delay once it has already happened
pitfalls: Responsibility for observations during a handover delay can be unclear between ambulance and ED staff → agree ownership explicitly before cycle 1
Small numbers if 60-minute-plus delays are rare (a good sign operationally, but limits audit power) → extend the collection period
Ambulance staff may be tied up with other calls during a queue → record which service (ambulance or ED) took each observation
Staff may see this as adding a role during an already unsafe situation → frame it as protecting patients, not adding paperwork
Gains fade once escalation pressure passes and the role is dropped informally → tie the role to a defined occupancy/queue-length trigger, not to memory
pearls: Use the trust's existing ambulance handover delay escalation policy meeting to close the loop
Recruit both an ED matron and an ambulance operations manager as joint audit owners
Keep the 60-minute delay threshold and 30-minute observation interval identical across both cycles
Track NEWS2 escalation events as the safety outcome that matters most, not just the observation count
effort: ~20 min per case from ambulance observation and ED tracking records
pass: A full set of vital sign observations is recorded at least every 30 minutes for every patient whose handover exceeds 60 minutes, with escalation to a senior clinician if NEWS2 rises
